rationale: Block 3 introduces the five sub-disciplines of pharmacology; this checks whether students can distinguish pharmacokinetics from pharmacodynamics, the most commonly confused pair.
Block 6 covers drug nomenclature; this tests the foundational rule that the generic name is the INN and should be used on prescriptions.
Block 7 compares routes of administration; this checks the critical clinical distinction that the IV route has 100% bioavailability because it bypasses all absorption barriers.
Block 5 covers drug formulations; enteric coating is a key pharmaceutical concept that students must understand to counsel patients correctly about tablet modification.
Block 5 covers absorption and bioavailability; the first-pass effect is the most clinically important factor reducing oral bioavailability and is tested here.
Block 11 teaches zero-order vs first-order kinetics and steady state; ethanol's zero-order kinetics is a classic Tripathi/KDT teaching point for this concept.
Block 5 distinguishes agonists, partial agonists, and antagonists; the concept of intrinsic activity differentiates these classes and is a core pharmacodynamics principle.
Block 10 covers rational drug combinations including synergism and antagonism; the classic aspirin-ibuprofen pharmacodynamic interaction is the key clinical application tested here.
Block 5 covers paediatric pharmacokinetics; chloramphenicol 'grey baby syndrome' is the definitive teaching case for neonatal glucuronidation immaturity from Tripathi/KDT.
Block 8 covers pregnancy pharmacotherapy; teratogenicity risk and FDA categories are core knowledge for the 'pharmacotherapy in pregnancy' section of PH1.10.
Block 5 teaches the A-E ADR classification; distinguishing Type A (dose-dependent, predictable) from Type B (idiosyncratic, dose-independent) is the foundational classification tested here.
Block 8 covers drug interactions; the rifampicin-oral contraceptive interaction (CYP induction reducing OCP efficacy) is a high-yield pharmacokinetic drug interaction from Tripathi/KDT.
